big: The Nifty 50 can reach you in two parcels: an index fund bought from the fund house, or an ETF bought on the stock exchange like a share. The index inside is the same. The way you buy is not.

lines: I have a demat account. Should I buy the Nifty ETF or the Nifty index fund?
Depends how you invest. Let us watch a monthly SIP first, then the hidden cost of trading an ETF.

h: An index fund SIP, month by month
alt: Six monthly instalments buying units of an index fund at changing prices
caps: The index fund is bought from the fund house at the day's NAV. No demat order is needed.
Each month the ₹5,000 instalment goes in automatically, at that day's NAV.
The NAV moves, and the units you get move the other way. The SIP just runs.
With an ETF you would place a buy order on the exchange every month. That is why the fund suits SIPs.

h: The hidden cost of trading an ETF
rows: Extra paid on a ₹10 lakh buy (₹)
alt: Bars comparing the extra price paid when buying a thinly traded ETF and a busy ETF
caps: An ETF trades at a market price. You buy at the price sellers ask, and sell at the price buyers bid.
The gap between the two is the spread. In a busy ETF it is tiny: about 2 basis points, or 0.02%.
In a thin ETF it can be wider. Here 40 basis points, or 0.4%. Both figures are examples.
On a ₹10 lakh buy that is ₹4,000 extra in the thin ETF against ₹200 in the busy one.

title: Fair claims, and unfair ones
stops: Index fund: bought at the day's NAV
ETF: needs a demat account and trades all day
An ETF always trades exactly at NAV
The wrapper decides the index return
alt: A shield with true and false statements about index funds and ETFs
caps: An index fund is priced at day's NAV by the AMC. An ETF trades all day on the exchange, with a demat.
The ETF price can differ slightly from NAV. The index inside is the same.
So the wrapper matters less than cost, tracking and, for an ETF, the spread.

q: Rohan wants a ₹5,000 SIP in a Nifty fund, running for ten years with no monthly effort. He has a demat account. Which is the simpler route?
opts: The ETF, since a demat account sets up the monthly buy itself
The index fund, since its SIP debits and buys on its own
The ETF, since it is always cheaper than an index fund
Either one, since both need a manual order each month
why: An ETF is bought on the exchange, so he has to place an order each month unless his broker offers a plan.
The fund house runs the SIP and buys units at NAV, so he does nothing after the mandate is set.
An ETF may have a lower expense ratio, but the spread and effort can cancel that. It is not always cheaper.
Only the ETF needs a manual order. The index fund is built for a standing monthly instruction.

q: Meena buys ₹5,00,000 of an ETF at its ask of ₹250 a unit. The NAV at that moment is ₹249. About how much more did she pay than the NAV value of what she bought?
opts: About ₹500, as the gap is about 0.1% of the buy
About ₹5,000, as an ETF buy always costs 1% extra
About ₹2,000: ₹1 more on each of 2,000 units
Nothing extra, since an ETF trades at NAV by rule
why: The gap is about 0.4%, not 0.1%. ₹1 on a ₹249 unit is 0.4%, and 0.4% of ₹5 lakh is ₹2,000.
No fixed 1% charge exists. The extra paid is whatever gap there is between price and NAV.
₹5,00,000 buys 2,000 units at ₹250. A ₹1 gap above NAV on each unit is ₹2,000, about 0.4%.
An ETF can trade a little above or below NAV. Here it traded above, and she paid for the gap.

q: Rohan will invest a ₹10 lakh lump sum for ten years. The ETF's expense ratio is 0.05% and its spread about 0.05% each time he trades. The index fund's expense ratio is 0.20% with no spread. Ignoring brokerage, which statement is right?
opts: The index fund costs less, since it has no spread to pay
They cost the same, since both follow the very same index
The ETF always costs more, since it trades on an exchange
The ETF likely costs less in total, if it stays liquid
why: No spread saves only about 0.1%, while the ETF's lower yearly cost saves about 1.5% over ten years.
Same index does not mean same cost. Expense ratio and spread differ, and they add up over years.
Trading adds a spread, but on a liquid ETF it is tiny. The lower yearly cost outweighs it.
Over ten years the ETF costs about 0.6% (expenses plus spreads) against 2% for the fund, by simple sums.

q: An ETF on the Nifty trades at ₹249.90 while its NAV is ₹250.00 near the close. A client asks if the ETF is broken. What is the sound reply?
opts: A small gap is normal in a busy ETF, if it stays small
Yes, since an ETF must trade at exactly its NAV all day
Yes, since the fund house is hiding losses until day end
No, since any gap, even one of 5%, would be normal
why: A gap of about 0.04% is within a normal spread. Thin ETFs can show wider gaps, so size and volume are worth a check.
No rule forces trading at NAV. Buyers and sellers set the price, and arbitrage keeps it close to the NAV.
NAV is computed from the value of the holdings, so the fund house cannot hide losses in this way.
A 5% gap would be a warning sign for liquidity. A gap of a few paise is the normal kind.

pts: Index fund: bought at NAV from the AMC, SIP-friendly. ETF: exchange, demat, market price.
The spread is the hidden cost of an ETF. Thin ETFs have wider spreads.
Same index. Judge by expense ratio, tracking difference and spread, not by the wrapper.
